body:
What makes genetic information sensitive?

Human genetic information consists of data about a person's DNA, genes or inherited biological characteristics. It may be generated through genetic testing, genome sequencing or research involving biological samples.

Unlike many ordinary records, genetic information can reveal characteristics that are relatively persistent throughout life. Some findings may indicate inherited health conditions, disease susceptibility or biological relationships.

Genetic information can also have implications for relatives because family members share portions of their inherited genetic material.

DNA samples and genetic data

A biological sample and the information obtained from it are related but distinct.

A blood or saliva sample may contain cells from which DNA can be analysed. A genetic test may then produce a digital record describing particular genetic variations or other findings.

Both the original sample and the resulting information may require appropriate ethical safeguards, but they are not the same material.

Privacy and confidentiality

Privacy

Privacy concerns an individual's interest in controlling access to personal information and aspects of personal life.

In genetic research, privacy includes respecting decisions about whether genetic information should be collected and how it may be used.

Confidentiality

Confidentiality is the responsibility to protect information entrusted to a researcher or healthcare professional from unauthorized disclosure.

For example, a researcher who receives an identifiable genetic result must protect that information in accordance with the participant's consent and applicable requirements.

A person may agree to testing without agreeing that the results may be disclosed to family members, employers or unrelated third parties.

Identifiable, coded and anonymized information

Genetic datasets may be handled in different forms.

  • Identifiable data: Information linked directly to a person's identity.
  • Coded or pseudonymized data: Direct identifiers are replaced with a code, while additional information may permit authorized re-identification.
  • Anonymized data: Information is processed so that the individual is no longer identifiable under the applicable standard.

Coding can reduce privacy risks, but it does not necessarily make information anonymous. In particular, detailed genetic information may remain sensitive because identification can sometimes become possible by combining datasets or using other available information.

Replacing a person's name with a code is not the same as guaranteeing anonymity. The possibility of re-identification must be considered when genetic information is shared.

Why genetic data require careful governance

Responsible governance addresses the full period during which samples or information are collected, stored, analysed, shared or retained.

Purpose and consent

Participants should understand the intended uses of their genetic information. A diagnostic test, a particular research study and later unrelated research may require different ethical considerations.

Authorized access

Access should be limited according to legitimate responsibilities and applicable approvals. Researchers must not assume that participation in one project gives every future investigator unrestricted access to identifiable information.

Secure storage and responsible sharing

Institutions should use appropriate safeguards to prevent unauthorized disclosure, loss or misuse. Sharing with other institutions requires consideration of consent, confidentiality and relevant regulatory conditions.

Retention and future use

Participants should receive suitable information about how long samples or information may be retained and whether future uses are anticipated.

Genetic information can affect relatives and communities

Suppose a research participant is found to carry a genetic variation associated with an inherited disease. That finding may have implications for biological relatives.

However, the possible usefulness of the information to relatives does not automatically eliminate the participant's confidentiality rights. Disclosure decisions require careful ethical consideration and must follow applicable rules.

Similarly, a population-level finding may create risks of discrimination or stigmatization if it is inaccurately presented as a characteristic of every person belonging to that community.

Incidental findings and the communication of results

An incidental finding is information discovered during a test or study that is outside its original purpose but may have potential significance.

For example, a broad genetic analysis undertaken for one research question may identify a different genetic variation of possible medical importance.

Whether and how such findings are communicated depends on factors such as their reliability, clinical significance, consent arrangements and ethical guidance. Appropriate counselling may be necessary to explain uncertainty and available choices.

The right not to know may also be relevant when participants are asked whether they wish to receive certain types of genetic information.

Fairness and genetic discrimination

Genetic information can indicate probabilities or susceptibilities rather than inevitable outcomes. Treating a person as certain to develop a disease solely because of a genetic risk indicator can be scientifically misleading.

Ethical governance seeks to reduce unjust discrimination, misuse of personal information and stigmatization. These concerns are especially important when genetic findings are interpreted outside their proper medical or scientific context.

Prelims focus

  • Genetic data can reveal information about individuals and biological relatives.
  • Privacy concerns control over personal information; confidentiality concerns protection against unauthorized disclosure.
  • Coded genetic data are not necessarily anonymous.
  • Consent for one genetic study does not automatically permit every future use.
  • Incidental findings may arise outside the original purpose of genetic testing.
  • Trap: A genetic predisposition generally indicates susceptibility, not certainty that a condition will develop.

[Sources: Indian Council of Medical Research, National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants, 2017, Section 10, Human Genetics Testing and Research, especially Sections 10.2–10.8, printed pp. 113–116; Section 11, Biological Materials, Biobanking and Datasets, printed pp. 127–136. Official ICMR publication consulted 13 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Genetic information requires protection because it may identify individuals and reveal familial connections.

title: Genetic Data Privacy, Confidentiality and Responsible Information Sharing

body:
Biological resources as a source of useful knowledge

Plants, animals, microorganisms and other biological resources provide valuable materials for agriculture, medicine and biotechnology.

Genetic resources contain hereditary information with actual or potential value. Research may investigate their genetic or biochemical characteristics to develop useful products or knowledge.

Many communities also possess traditional knowledge about biological resources, including their identification, conservation and customary uses.

When such resources or knowledge contribute to research and commercialization, questions arise about lawful access, recognition of knowledge holders and fair distribution of benefits.

Meaning of access and benefit-sharing

Access and benefit-sharing (ABS) refers to arrangements governing access to genetic resources and the fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from their utilization, in accordance with applicable rules and agreed conditions.

ABS aims to ensure that the use of biological resources does not unfairly exclude the countries or communities entitled to participate in the benefits.

Two important ABS concepts

Prior informed consent

Prior informed consent (PIC) means obtaining the required authorization before accessing genetic resources or associated traditional knowledge where applicable law requires such authorization.

Under international ABS arrangements, the relevant consent or approval may involve the providing country and, where required under domestic law, indigenous or local communities.

The precise procedure depends on the applicable national legislation and the rights recognized under it.

Mutually agreed terms

Mutually agreed terms (MAT) are agreed conditions governing the use of resources and the sharing of resulting benefits.

They may address matters such as permitted purposes, commercialization, payments, access to research results and other agreed benefits.

PIC concerns authorization to access a resource; MAT concerns the agreed conditions for its use and benefit-sharing. Both concepts are central to the Nagoya Protocol's ABS framework.

Monetary and non-monetary benefits

Benefit-sharing does not necessarily involve only cash payments.

Benefit typeExamples
MonetaryAgreed payments, royalties or financial contributions
Non-monetarySharing research results, knowledge, training or technology according to agreed terms

The appropriate form of benefit-sharing depends on the resource, applicable law and mutually agreed conditions. Neither a fixed royalty nor a particular research partnership is universally required for every situation.

The relationship between access, utilization and benefits

Consider a hypothetical research organization seeking to investigate a plant associated with a community's traditional knowledge.

Where ABS requirements apply, the organization must follow the relevant access procedures and obtain required authorization. The conditions governing permitted utilization and benefit-sharing must then be established as applicable.

If the research subsequently produces commercially valuable results, benefit-sharing is determined through the relevant legal and agreed arrangements.

What is biopiracy?

Biopiracy generally refers to the unauthorized or unfair exploitation of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge, particularly where required authorization, recognition or fair benefit-sharing is absent.

For example, commercial exploitation of a biological resource associated with longstanding community knowledge, without complying with applicable access requirements, may raise biopiracy concerns.

However, not every scientific study of a naturally occurring organism is automatically biopiracy, and not every patent involving biotechnology is unlawful. The relevant facts, applicable law and rights of resource providers must be examined.

The Convention on Biological Diversity

The Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) was opened for signature at the Rio Earth Summit in 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993.

It has 3 main objectives:

  1. Conservation of biological diversity.
  2. Sustainable use of the components of biological diversity.
  3. Fair and equitable sharing of benefits arising from the utilization of genetic resources.

The CBD recognizes the sovereign rights of countries over their natural resources and provides the broader international framework for access and benefit-sharing.

The Nagoya Protocol

The Nagoya Protocol on Access to Genetic Resources and the Fair and Equitable Sharing of Benefits Arising from Their Utilization was adopted on 29 October 2010 and entered into force on 12 October 2014.

It supplements the CBD by establishing a more detailed international framework for access, benefit-sharing and compliance with applicable access requirements.

The Protocol also addresses traditional knowledge associated with genetic resources, subject to its provisions and applicable domestic laws.

India's Biological Diversity Act

India enacted the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 to support biodiversity conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable benefit-sharing.

The legislation establishes an institutional framework involving the National Biodiversity Authority, State Biodiversity Boards and Biodiversity Management Committees.

The Biological Diversity (Amendment) Act, 2023 introduced changes intended to simplify certain compliance arrangements, clarify institutional responsibilities and address aspects of the Nagoya Protocol.

At the content cutoff of 13 November 2026, the National Biodiversity Authority's official guidance identifies the Biological Diversity Rules, 2024, effective from 21 December 2024, as having superseded the 2004 Rules. It also identifies the Biological Diversity (Amendment) Rules, 2025, effective from 1 November 2025.

The amended framework contains specific procedures and exemptions. Therefore, it is incorrect to assume that all access to biological resources requires identical approvals or that all commercial uses are automatically exempt from benefit-sharing obligations.

ABS consent and medical consent are different

Consent for access to a genetic resource under the Nagoya framework is not the same as informed consent from a human participant in a medical study.

ABS concerns lawful access to covered genetic resources and associated traditional knowledge. Medical research consent concerns an individual's voluntary participation and the authorized use of personal samples or information.

Although both involve consent and fairness, their purposes, legal frameworks and decision-making processes differ.

Prelims focus

  • CBD: 1992; objectives include conservation, sustainable use and fair benefit-sharing.
  • Nagoya Protocol: adopted in 2010; entered into force in 2014.
  • PIC means prior informed consent; MAT means mutually agreed terms.
  • Benefits may be monetary or non-monetary.
  • India's principal biodiversity legislation is the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, as amended.
  • Trap: The Nagoya Protocol addresses access and benefit-sharing, not the environmental release approval of genetically engineered organisms.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 12, Biotechnology and its Applications, Section 12.4, Ethical Issues, printed pp. 213–214; Convention on Biological Diversity, Nagoya Protocol, Articles 5–7 and About the Nagoya Protocol; National Biodiversity Authority, India, FAQs, questions 1–10, including the 2023 amendment and the 2024 and 2025 Rules. Official online sources consulted 13 November 2026; legal status stated at that cutoff.]
